translation.text: In the second year of the reign of Darius, Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo, the prophets, prophesied to the Jews who were in Judea[a] and Jerusalem in the name of the Lord God of Israel, to them[b].

footnotes.text: Or 'Judah' for 'Judea'; the Greek regional name is Ἰουδαία.
The closing ἐπ’ αὐτούς may also be understood as 'over them' or 'concerning them.' The main wording 'to them' is retained; the compressed phrase is not resolved by this source-import repair.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The temporal phrase is retained as 'In the second year'; connective δέ is carried by the narrative context.
βασιλεία here denotes kingship/reign rather than the abstract 'kingdom.' The genitive construction is most naturally rendered 'of the reign of Darius.'
The aorist verb is the standard term for prophetic activity. English 'prophesied' is both accurate and natural.

The closing phrase 'over them' could also be understood as 'concerning them' or, less likely in context, simply 'to them.' The Greek and Hebrew both preserve this somewhat compressed wording.
The Greek text has a duplicated article before 'prophets' ('the the prophets'), likely a scribal or transmission irregularity; the translation gives the intended sense.

lexical_decisions.rationale: δέ is lightly connective; 'Now' preserves narrative progression without overtranslating. The temporal dative phrase is rendered straightforwardly. βασιλεία here denotes kingship/reign rather than the abstract 'kingdom.' The genitive construction is most naturally rendered 'of the reign of Darius.'

lexical_decisions.source_word: Ἀγγαῖος καὶ Ζαχαρίας ὁ τοῦ Ἐδδεὶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo
alternatives: Haggai and Zechariah the son of Iddin/Iddo
Haggai and Zechariah, son of Iddo
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek reflects the Semitic patronymic also seen in the MT parallel (בַר־עִדּוֹא). Standard English biblical name form is 'Iddo.' The singular patronymic most naturally modifies Zechariah, not both prophets.

Despite the duplicated article in Swete's text, the sense is plainly appositional/plural: Haggai and Zechariah are identified as 'the prophets.' The duplication is best treated as a textual irregularity, not represented in translation.

With verbs of speaking/prophesying, ἐπί can mark direction toward an audience or object. The MT parallel עַל־יְהוּדָיֵא likewise supports prophetic address directed to them, not hostility against them.

translation.text: Let everything be known to our lord the king: when we came into the land of Judea and to Jerusalem, the city, we found the elders of the captivity of the Jews[a] in Jerusalem, the city, building a great new house for the Lord[b], with costly hewn stones, with timber laid in the buildings,

footnotes.text: Or, more literally, 'the elders of the Jews of the captivity.' The Greek wording is compressed; the sense is the leadership of the Jewish exile/returnee community.
'House for the Lord' refers to the temple.

alternatives: Be it known in every respect
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase is an epistolary/report formula. 'Let everything be known' preserves the imperative force of ἔστω with natural English while keeping the breadth of πάντα.

alternatives: to our sovereign lord the king
lexical_decisions.rationale: κύριος here is a courtly title for the Persian king, not a divine title. 'Lord' follows the project's default for κύριος and fits the deferential register; 'our lord the king' preserves both nouns.
The participle is temporal in context, introducing the circumstances of the report. 'When we came' is idiomatic and sufficiently close to the Greek.
χώρα can mean land, region, or territory. 'Land of Judea' is broad and avoids over-specifying an administrative nuance not explicit in the Greek.
The appositional wording is somewhat repetitive in Greek and is retained in a lightly smoothed form to reflect the source's emphasis.
In this context the verb means 'found/encountered' rather than 'seized.' The object is the elders engaged in building, so 'we found' best fits the sense.
The existing English retains the literal captivity wording in the compressed phrase identifying the Jewish elders; a smoother exilic-community alternative remains in the note.

alternatives: the elders of the Jews of the exile
the Jewish elders of the captivity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The elder/Jew wording is retained, with τῆς αἰχμαλωσίας represented as 'of the captivity' in the intervening English phrase. The note gives the alternative ordering without changing the main.
οἶκος literally means 'house.' Because the dative τῷ κυρίῳ marks it as God's house, 'house for the Lord' preserves the temple reference without importing 'temple' where the Greek says 'house.'
Here κύριος refers to Israel's God. Per doctrine, it is rendered 'Lord.' 'For the Lord' fits the construction with οἶκον in English.
Both adjectives modify οἶκον. 'Great new house' preserves both descriptors straightforwardly; 'magnificent' would over-interpret μέγαν.

λίθοι are stones; ξυστῶν here describes worked/dressed stone rather than raw fieldstone; πολυτελῶν adds the sense of costly or luxurious quality. 'Hewn stones' is natural English for worked building stone and stays close to the construction context.

alternatives: wood being set in the houses
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξύλων is best rendered 'timber/wood'; τιθεμένων is a participle meaning being placed or laid; οἴκοις in this construction refers to the building structures/rooms rather than domestic houses specifically. 'Timber laid in the buildings' preserves the construction imagery.

translation.text: and those works being done with diligence[a], and the work prospering in their hands, being completed with all glory[b] and care.

footnotes.text: Or 'with haste' for 'with diligence'; the Greek phrase ἐπὶ σπουδῆς can emphasize urgency as well as earnest care.
'Glory' here likely carries the sense of splendor or magnificence in the workmanship, not only honor in an abstract sense.

lexical_decisions.source_word: τὰ ἔργα ἐκεῖνα ἐπὶ σπουδῆς γινόμενα
lexical_decisions.chosen: those works being done with diligence
alternatives: those works being done with haste
those works being carried out earnestly
lexical_decisions.rationale: σπουδή can denote eagerness, diligence, earnestness, and in some contexts haste. In a royal building report, 'with diligence' best captures careful energetic execution without implying recklessness.

lexical_decisions.source_word: εὐοδούμενον τὸ ἔργον ἐν ταῖς χερσὶν αὐτῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the work prospering in their hands
alternatives: the work succeeding in their hands
the work advancing under their hands
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐοδόω means to prosper or succeed. The idiom 'in their hands' is retained because it is transparent in English and reflects the source's agency idiom.
